name: Roman Green
lede: Roman green is a muted olive. The name belongs to two things: a dull green swatch in the old color atlases, and a 19th-century artists' pigment.

sections.title: The artists' pigment
sections.body:
The *Pigment Compendium* quotes Salter, writing in 1869, that a President of the Royal Academy had carried Roman green home from Rome, and that it looked like Prussian blue blended with Dutch or Italian pink [1]. Dutch and Italian pinks were yellow lake pigments, so this was a blue and yellow mixture [1]. The compendium gives it a short entry resting on that one source [1].

The name should not be read as Roman taste, since Pastoureau notes that for the Romans themselves, green, and blue even more, was a barbarian color [2].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch #6F7044 comes from the color atlases: Ridgway's 1912 plate XVI, Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, and the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955, which calls it a light grayish olive [3]. It is a different thing from Salter's pigment, and the books do not connect them [1][3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is common in painting: our archive of 23,781 has it in 1,101 works (4.63%), as photographed [4]. The earliest match is from the 900s, a thousand years before Ridgway's name, so these are look-alike hues in aged paint [4]. Peter Snayers is its most devoted painter, with it in 6 of 16 works [4]. Neighbors are [[olive-green]], [[olive]] and [[khaki]] [3].
